claim: Venus-tagged Wnt8 was found on the surfaces of cells close to Wnt-producing cells.
source: While Venus-tagged Wnt8 was found on the surfaces of cells close to Wnt-producing cells, we also detected its dispersal over distances of 15 cell diameters.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a direct observation from the experiments.

claim: Venus-tagged Wnt8 disperses over distances of 15 cell diameters.
source: While Venus-tagged Wnt8 was found on the surfaces of cells close to Wnt-producing cells, we also detected its dispersal over distances of 15 cell diameters.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a direct observation from the experiments.

claim: Only a small proportion of Wnt8 ligands diffuses freely.
source: A combination of fluorescence correlation spectroscopy and quantitative imaging suggested that only a small proportion of Wnt8 ligands diffuses freely, whereas most Wnt8 molecules are bound to cell surfaces.
evidence: This conclusion is based on FCS and quantitative imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Most Wnt8 molecules are bound to cell surfaces.
source: A combination of fluorescence correlation spectroscopy and quantitative imaging suggested that only a small proportion of Wnt8 ligands diffuses freely, whereas most Wnt8 molecules are bound to cell surfaces.
evidence: This conclusion is based on FCS and quantitative imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Wnt8 ligands bound on cell surfaces decrease exponentially after photoconversion.
source: Fluorescence decay after photoconversion showed that Wnt8 ligands bound on cell surfaces decrease exponentially, suggesting a dynamic exchange of bound forms of Wnt ligands.
evidence: This is based on FDAP experimental data showing exponential decay.

claim: There is a dynamic exchange of bound forms of Wnt ligands.
source: Fluorescence decay after photoconversion showed that Wnt8 ligands bound on cell surfaces decrease exponentially, suggesting a dynamic exchange of bound forms of Wnt ligands.
evidence: This is inferred from the exponential decay observed in FDAP experiments.

claim: Mathematical modeling based on dynamic exchange recapitulates a graded distribution of bound Wnt ligands.
source: Mathematical modeling based on this exchange recapitulates a graded distribution of bound, but not free, Wnt ligands.
evidence: This is based on mathematical modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mathematical modeling based on dynamic exchange does not recapitulate a graded distribution of free Wnt ligands.
source: Mathematical modeling based on this exchange recapitulates a graded distribution of bound, but not free, Wnt ligands.
evidence: This is based on mathematical modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Wnt distribution in tissues is controlled by a dynamic exchange of abundant bound and rare free populations.
source: Based on these results, we propose that Wnt distribution in tissues is controlled by a dynamic exchange of its abundant bound and rare free populations.
evidence: This is the main proposal of the paper based on the experimental and modeling data.

claim: Morphogenic Wnt ligands form a concentration gradient by dispersal in the extracellular space.
source: It has been generally accepted that in the extracellular space, morphogenic Wnt ligands form a concentration gradient by dispersal (Clevers et al., 2014; Kiecker and Niehrs, 2001; Müller et al., 2013; Smith, 2009; Strigini and Cohen, 2000; Tabata and Takei, 2004; Yan and Lin, 2009; Zecca et al., 1996; Zhu and Scott, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations from the literature.

claim: A membrane-tethered form of Wingless can recapitulate an almost normal pattern of Drosophila wings.
source: For instance, a membrane-tethered form of Wingless (Wg) can recapitulate an almost normal pattern of Drosophila wings, suggesting that dispersal of Wg is dispensable for patterning (Alexandre et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Alexandre et al., 2014.

claim: Dispersal of Wingless is dispensable for patterning in Drosophila wings.
source: For instance, a membrane-tethered form of Wingless (Wg) can recapitulate an almost normal pattern of Drosophila wings, suggesting that dispersal of Wg is dispensable for patterning (Alexandre et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that membrane-tethered Wg can recapitulate normal patterning.

claim: Wg proteins are widely distributed from wing margin cells in the wing disc of Drosophila.
source: In the wing disc of Drosophila, Wg proteins are widely distributed from wing margin cells, where Wg is expressed (Strigini and Cohen, 2000; Zecca et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Strigini and Cohen, 2000 and Zecca et al., 1996.

claim: Long-range dispersal of Wg was evidenced by an experiment in which Wg was captured by distally expressed Frizzled2.
source: Furthermore, long-range dispersal of Wg was evidenced by an experiment in which Wg was captured by distally expressed Frizzled2, a Wg receptor (Chaudhary et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chaudhary et al., 2019.

claim: Endogenous Wnt ligands tagged with fluorescent proteins showed long-range distributions in C. elegans.
source: Similarly, endogenous Wnt ligands tagged with fluorescent proteins showed long-range distributions in C. elegans (Pani and Goldstein, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pani and Goldstein, 2018.

claim: Endogenous Wnt8 ligands disperse far from their source cells in Xenopus embryos.
source: In addition to these observations in invertebrates, we found that endogenous Wnt8 ligands disperse far from their source cells in Xenopus embryos (Mii et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Mouse Wnt3 accumulates within a few cell diameters of its source cells in the microenvironment of the intestine.
source: On the other hand, mouse Wnt3 accumulates within a few cell diameters of its source cells in the microenvironment of the intestine (Farin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Farin et al., 2016.

claim: Wnt ligands accumulate locally on cell surfaces, showing punctate distributional patterns.
source: Importantly, in many of these studies, Wnt ligands accumulate locally on cell surfaces, showing punctate distributional patterns (Pani and Goldstein, 2018; Strigini and Cohen, 2000; Zecca et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations from the literature.

claim: Wnt8 and Frzb accumulate separately and locally on cell surfaces in Xenopus embryos.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrated that Wnt8 and Frzb, a secreted Wnt inhibitor, accumulate separately and locally on cell surfaces in Xenopus embryos (Mii et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Cell surface scaffolds, such as heparan sulfate proteoglycans, are required for both distribution and delivery of morphogens in Drosophila wing disc.
source: Studies in Drosophila wing disc have shown that cell surface scaffolds, such as heparan sulfate (HS) proteoglycans (HSPGs), are required for both distribution and delivery of morphogens, including Wg, Hedgehog (Hh), and Decapentaplegic (Dpp) (Franch-Marro et al., 2005; Lin, 2004; Yan and Lin, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations from the literature.

claim: HSPGs on cell surfaces are discretely distributed in a punctate manner in Xenopus embryos.
source: On the other hand, we recently showed that HSPGs on cell surfaces are discretely distributed in a punctate manner, which varies with heparan sulfate (HS) modification, forming two different types of HS clusters, N-sulfo-rich and N-acetyl-rich forms (Mii et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Wnt8 and Frzb accumulate separately on N-sulfo-rich and N-acetyl-rich HS clusters, respectively.
source: Notably, Wnt8 and Frzb, a secreted Frizzled-related protein (sFRP), accumulate separately on N-sulfo-rich and N-acetyl-rich HS clusters, respectively.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the authors' previous work.

claim: Frzb expands the distribution and signaling range of Wnt8 by forming heterocomplexes.
source: Frzb expands the distribution and signaling range of Wnt8 by forming heterocomplexes (Mii and Taira, 2009), and Wnt8/Frzb complexes are colocalized with N-acetyl-rich HS clusters (Mii et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the authors' previous work.

claim: N-sulfo-rich clusters are frequently internalized together with Wnt8.
source: N-sulfo-rich clusters are frequently internalized together with Wnt8, whereas N-acetyl-rich HS clusters tend to remain on the cell surface.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the authors' previous work.

claim: N-acetyl-rich HS clusters tend to remain on the cell surface.
source: N-sulfo-rich clusters are frequently internalized together with Wnt8, whereas N-acetyl-rich HS clusters tend to remain on the cell surface.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the authors' previous work.

claim: FRAP measurements showed that Dpp and Wg diffuse slowly in the Drosophila wing disc with diffusion coefficients ranging from 0.05 to 0.10 μm2/s.
source: For example, FRAP measurements have shown that Dpp and Wg diffuse slowly in the Drosophila wing disc with diffusion coefficients ranging from 0.05 to 0.10 μm2/s, suggestive of the restricted diffusion model (Kicheva et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kicheva et al., 2007.

claim: FCS measurements of FGF8 in zebrafish embryos showed fast, virtually free diffusion, with a diffusion coefficient of ~50 μm2/s.
source: In contrast, FCS measurements of FGF8 in zebrafish embryos showed fast, virtually free diffusion, with a diffusion coefficient of ~50 μm2/s (Yu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yu et al., 2009.

claim: Free diffusion of Dpp measured in the Drosophila wing disc using FCS yielded a diffusion coefficient of ~20 μm2/s.
source: Furthermore, in contrast to the FRAP results, free diffusion of Dpp measured in the Drosophila wing disc using FCS yielded a diffusion coefficient of ~20 μm2/s (Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhou et al., 2012.

claim: mV-Wnt8 and mV-Frzb were visualized along cell boundaries when expressed in Xenopus embryos.
source: As we have previously shown (Mii et al., 2017), Wnt8 and Frzb fused with monomeric Venus (mV) were visualized along cell boundaries when expressed in Xenopus embryos (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Biological activities of mV-tagged Wnt8 and Frzb were not severely impaired by the fusion of mV.
source: We note that biological activities of these proteins were not severely impaired by the fusion of mV and that the reduced activity of mV-tagged Wnt8 compared to untagged Wnt8 could possibly be due, at least in part, to differences in translation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The secreted form of mV (sec-mV) was hardly visible along the cell boundary under the same conditions as mV-Wnt8 and mV-Frzb.
source: In contrast, we found that only the secreted form of mV (sec-mV), which was not expected to bind specifically to the cell surface, was hardly visible along the cell boundary under the same conditions (Figure 1A, right).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Addition of heparin-binding peptides to sec-mV significantly increased the intensity of mVenus fluorescence in the intercellular region compared to that of sec-mV.
source: Addition of HB peptides significantly increased the intensity of mVenus fluorescence in the intercellular region compared to that of sec-mV.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the experiments with HB peptides.

claim: The intercellular distribution of secreted proteins depends on interactions with docking molecules on cell surfaces.
source: This suggests that the intercellular distribution of secreted proteins depends on interactions with docking molecules on cell surfaces.
evidence: This is inferred from the HB peptide experiments.

claim: sec-mV-2HA was hardly visible in the intercellular space, even close to the source cells.
source: As with sec-mV, sec-mV-2HA was hardly visible in the intercellular space, even close to the source cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: sec-mV-2HA was observed around tethered-anti-HA Ab-expressing cells that were distantly located from the source cells.
source: In contrast, sec-mV-2HA was observed around tethered-anti-HA Ab-expressing cells that were traced with memRFP, even though these cells were distantly located from the source cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Interaction with cell surface proteins can affect distributions of secreted proteins.
source: Thus, interaction with cell surface proteins can affect distributions of secreted proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the tethered-anti-HA Ab experiments.

claim: Diffusing proteins are not readily visible using standard confocal microscopy, unless they are trapped by cell surface proteins.
source: This result also indicates that diffusing proteins are not readily visible using standard confocal microscopy, unless they are trapped by cell surface proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the tethered-anti-HA Ab experiments.

claim: sec-mV accumulated on the surface of morphotrap-expressing cells remote from source cells.
source: As expected, sec-mV accumulated on the surface of morphotrap-expressing cells remote from source cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: mV-Wnt8 and mV-Frzb were trapped by morphotrap-expressing cells over 15 cells/200 μm from source cells.
source: Similarly, mV-Wnt8 and mV-Frzb were trapped (Figure 2C), evidencing the long-distance dispersal (over 15 cells/200 μm) of some of secreted mV-Wnt8 and mV-Frzb molecules.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: mV-Wnt8 and mV-Frzb were detectable in gradients from producing cells to morphotrap-expressing cells.
source: In addition to this dispersing population, mV-Wnt8 and mV-Frzb were also detectable in gradients from producing cells to morphotrap-expressing cells, unlike the case of sec-mV (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: Populations of mV-tagged Wnt8 and Frzb do not associate tightly with cell surfaces, thereby potentially dispersing far from source cells.
source: These results suggest that populations of mV-tagged Wnt8 and Frzb do not associate tightly with cell surfaces, thereby potentially dispersing far from source cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the morphotrap experiments.

claim: The number of particles (NoP) of mV-Wnt8 (250 pg/embryo) was significantly higher than that of mV-Wnt8 (20 pg/embryo, endogenous-equivalent level).
source: Consistent with predictions, the result indicated that the number of particles (NoP) of mV-Wnt8 (250 pg/embryo) was significantly higher than that of mV-Wnt8 (20 pg/embryo, endogenous-equivalent level; Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Fast-diffusing components in all groups examined can be regarded as free diffusion.
source: Mean values of Dfast indicate that fast-diffusing components in all groups examined can be regarded as free diffusion (Figure 3D), because theoretical, as well as reported D values of freely diffusing proteins of similar size, range from 10 to 100 μm2/s (Pack et al., 2006; Yu et al., 2009; Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on FCS data in Figure 3D and comparison with literature values.

claim: At the endogenous-equivalent level, mV-Wnt8 and mV-Frzb show freely diffusing populations (Dfast >10 μm2/s).
source: Importantly, even at the endogenous-equivalent level, mV-Wnt8 and mV-Frzb show freely diffusing populations (Dfast >10 μm2/s, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The diffusion coefficient of the fast component of mV-Wnt8 (20 pg/embryo, endogenous-equivalent level) was significantly lower than that of mV-Wnt8 (250 pg/embryo).
source: We also note that the diffusion coefficient of the fast component of mV-Wnt8 (20 pg/embryo, endogenous-equivalent level) was significantly lower than that of mV-Wnt8 (250 pg/embryo), suggesting stronger constraints with the endogenous-equivalent expression level.
evidence: This is based on FCS data comparing different expression levels.

claim: A population of mV-Wnt8 and mV-Frzb molecules diffuses freely under physiological conditions.
source: Thus, we conclude that within the small volume of FCS measurements, a population of mV-Wnt8 and mV-Frzb molecules diffuses freely under physiological conditions.
evidence: This is concluded from FCS measurements.

claim: NoP of mV-Wnt8 was similar to that of sec-mV under the same conditions (250 pg mRNA/embryo).
source: However, under the same conditions as in Figure 1 (250 pg mRNA/embryo), NoP of mV-Wnt8 was similar to that of sec-mV (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) or even smaller in another set of measurements (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Molecules detected in FCS appear not to contribute to the photon counts in the confocal imaging under these conditions.
source: Thus, molecules detected in FCS appear not to contribute to the photon counts in the confocal imaging under these conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of FCS and imaging data.

claim: For mV-Wnt8, NoP and the fraction of fast components (Ffast) was significantly increased by HepIII.
source: For mV-Wnt8, NoP and the fraction of fast components, Ffast was significantly increased by HepIII, suggesting release of mV-Wnt8 from HS chains (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 3E and 3F.

claim: HS chains contribute to the slow components of mV-Wnt8.
source: Thus, we suggest that HS chains contribute to the slow components of mV-Wnt8.
evidence: This is inferred from the HepIII digestion experiments.

claim: For sec-mV, Ffast was slightly, but significantly increased by HepIII.
source: For sec-mV, although NoP was not significantly changed by HepIII, Ffast was slightly, but significantly increased by HepIII (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 3G and 3H.

claim: FCCS analysis indicated that sec-mV did not interact with the cell membrane.
source: Furthermore, fluorescence cross-correlation spectroscopy (FCCS) analysis indicated that sec-mV did not interact with the cell membrane (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: HS-chains showed some contribution to the slow components of sec-mV even without interaction.
source: Thus, HS-chains showed some contribution to the slow components of sec-mV even without interaction.
evidence: This is inferred from the HepIII and FCCS experiments.

claim: The slow population of sec-mV could be explained by hindered diffusion.
source: We speculate that such a slow population of sec-mV could be explained by hindered diffusion, in which torturous diffusion results from HS chains and other ECMs, because HS chains are highly hydrophilic and well hydrated (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is speculated based on the properties of HS chains.

claim: mK-Wnt8 and mK-Frzb showed distributions in embryos similar to mV-tagged proteins.
source: These fusion proteins showed distributions in embryos similar to mV-tagged proteins (Figure 4A), and retained biological activities (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: mK-Wnt8 and mK-Frzb retained biological activities.
source: These fusion proteins showed distributions in embryos similar to mV-tagged proteins (Figure 4A), and retained biological activities (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Observed distribution patterns of mK-Wnt8 and mK-Frzb were stable for up to tens of minutes.
source: Importantly, observed distribution patterns of mK-Wnt8 and mK-Frzb were stable for up to tens of minutes (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: mK-Wnt8 and mK-Frzb showed faster decline of fluorescent intensities compared with the fixed control.
source: Compared with this fixed control, mK-Wnt8 and mK-Frzb showed faster decline of fluorescent intensities (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), confirming that a population of mK-Wnt8 and mK-Frzb moved away from the photoconverted area.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: A population of mK-Wnt8 and mK-Frzb moved away from the photoconverted area.
source: Compared with this fixed control, mK-Wnt8 and mK-Frzb showed faster decline of fluorescent intensities (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), confirming that a population of mK-Wnt8 and mK-Frzb moved away from the photoconverted area.
evidence: This is inferred from the FDAP data.

claim: Bleaching-corrected FDAP curves of mK-Wnt8 and mK-Frzb were well fitted to the dissociation model.
source: Indeed, bleaching-corrected FDAP curves of mK-Wnt8 and mK-Frzb were well fitted to this model (Figure 4D; residuals were mostly within 5% and all within 10%) with the indicated parameters (Figure 4E, the off-rate constant koff, and the rate of the constantly bound component C; for individual data plot, see Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 4D and 4E.

claim: Both mK-Wnt8 and mK-Frzb show large C values, indicating that the majority of these proteins can be considered immobile on the timescale of the measurement.
source: As a result, both mK-Wnt8 and mK-Frzb show large C values, indicating that the majority of these proteins can be considered immobile on the timescale of the measurement (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E.

claim: koff of mK-Wnt8 was significantly lower than that of mK-Frzb.
source: In addition, koff of mK-Wnt8 was significantly lower than that of mK-Frzb (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D), suggesting relatively rapid dissociation of mK-Frzb from the binding site.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Most mK-Wnt8 and mK-Frzb molecules are bound, but can be exchanged with unbound molecules.
source: Thus, we conclude that most mK-Wnt8 and mK-Frzb molecules are bound, but can be exchanged with unbound molecules, and also dissociation rate values of mK-Wnt8 and mK-Frzb differ significantly.
evidence: This is concluded from the FDAP data.

claim: Dissociation rate values of mK-Wnt8 and mK-Frzb differ significantly.
source: Thus, we conclude that most mK-Wnt8 and mK-Frzb molecules are bound, but can be exchanged with unbound molecules, and also dissociation rate values of mK-Wnt8 and mK-Frzb differ significantly.
evidence: This is concluded from the FDAP data.

claim: Most Wnt8 and Frzb molecules distributed among cells are mostly cell-surface-bound, while a small portion of them are diffusing.
source: Based on quantitative live-imaging techniques, we propose that most Wnt8 molecules distributed among cells are mostly cell-surface-bound, while a small portion of them are diffusing.
evidence: This is the main conclusion based on the quantitative imaging, FCS, and FDAP data.

claim: Wnt/EGL-20 shows that puncta mostly overlap with Frizzled and a small population of mobile/diffusing molecules is also suggested in C. elegans.
source: Similarly, Wnt/EGL-20 shows that puncta mostly overlap with Frizzled and a small population of mobile/diffusing molecules is also suggested in C. elegans (Pani and Goldstein, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pani and Goldstein, 2018.

claim: A small population of diffusing Dpp has been shown in Drosophila wing disc.
source: Furthermore, a small population of diffusing Dpp has been shown in Drosophila wing disc (Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhou et al., 2012.

claim: Cell-surface-bound Wnt8 is mostly associated with HS clusters.
source: It is plausible that cell-surface-bound Wnt8 is mostly associated with HS clusters (Mii et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Most photoconverted mK-Wnt8 does not diffuse laterally, even when other puncta of Wnt8 exist near the site of photoconversion.
source: In our FDAP assay, most photoconverted mK-Wnt8 does not diffuse laterally, even when other puncta of Wnt8 exist near the site of photoconversion (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C, left panel, Video 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C and Video 1.

claim: mK-Frzb showed some lateral dispersal similar to the model.
source: On the other hand, mK-Frzb showed some lateral dispersal similar to the model.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the FDAP experiments.

claim: The apparent diffusion coefficient Da (μm2/s) was calculated as 0.042 and 0.059 for mKikGR-Wnt8 and mKikGR-Frzb, respectively.
source: As a result, the apparent diffusion coefficient Da (μm2/s) was calculated as 0.042 and 0.059 for mKikGR-Wnt8 and mKikGR-Frzb, respectively.
evidence: This is calculated from curve-fitting with the effective/apparent diffusion model.

claim: These values of Da are very close to a previously reported FRAP value for Wg (0.05 μm2/s).
source: These values are very close to a previously reported FRAP value for Wg (0.05 μm2/s) (Kicheva et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a comparison with literature values.

claim: sec-mV is almost invisible with standard confocal microscopy.
source: We found that sec-mV is almost invisible with standard confocal microscopy (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Binding to cell surface molecules such as HSPGs and membrane-tethered antibody was sufficient for visible distribution for artificial secreted proteins.
source: Furthermore, binding to cell surface molecules such as HSPGs and membrane-tethered antibody was sufficient for visible distribution for artificial secreted proteins (Figures 1C and 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 1C and 2B.

claim: Secreted GFP can be synthetic morphogens with specific scaffold molecules in the Drosophila wing disc.
source: These findings are similar to recent demonstrations that secreted GFP can be synthetic morphogens with specific scaffold molecules in the Drosophila wing disc (Stapornwongkul et al., 2020) and in cultured cells (Toda et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: Cell-boundary FDAP suggests that cell-surface-bound and diffusing populations are probably exchangeable.
source: Our cell-boundary FDAP suggests that cell-surface-bound and diffusing populations are probably exchangeable.
evidence: This is inferred from the FDAP data.

claim: When dissociation from the cell-surface does not occur (b = 0), the range of the gradient (decay length, λ) was shortened from 6.35 to 4.50 μm.
source: In our mathematical model, when dissociation from the cell-surface does not occur (b = 0 in Equation 3 and 4, Figure 5A), the range of the gradient (decay length, λ) was shortened from 6.35 to 4.50 μm (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Dissociation from the bound state seems to contribute to the long-range distribution and rapid formation of the gradient.
source: Thus, at least in cases we analyzed, dissociation from the bound state seems to contribute to the long-range distribution and rapid formation of the gradient.
evidence: This is inferred from the mathematical modeling results.

claim: Distributions of both free and bound components converged to steady states within a few minutes in the mathematical model.
source: Notably, in our mathematical model, distributions of both free and bound components converged to steady states within a few minutes, showing rather fast dynamics in the context of embryonic patterning.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the mathematical modeling.

claim: The combination of abundant cell-surface-bound and minimal diffusing populations would be beneficial for signaling stability and speed of pattern formation, respectively.
source: From this point of view, the combination of abundant cell-surface-bound and minimal diffusing populations would be beneficial for signaling stability and speed of pattern formation, respectively.
evidence: This is speculated based on the modeling results.

claim: Atypical distributions can be reproduced if specific scaffolds for ligands (ligand binding proteins) are anchored on the surfaces of cells.
source: In our model, atypical distributions can be reproduced if specific scaffolds for ligands (ligand binding proteins) are anchored on the surfaces of cells (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The model accounts for accumulations of ligand in regions lacking HS.
source: Distributional patterns of these ligands are explained by our model, which accounts for accumulations of ligand in regions lacking HS (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The model provides a basic framework to understand of the extracellular behavior of secreted proteins.
source: Thus, our model provides a basic framework to understand of the extracellular behavior of secreted proteins.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the modeling section.

claim: A smaller value of c results in long-range distribution in the mathematical model.
source: A smaller value of c results in long-range distribution (compare Figure 5B and C), explaining why Frzb shows a long-range distribution by binding to N-acetyl-rich HS clusters (Mii et al., 2017).
evidence: This is shown by comparing Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: The value of λ with c = 0.1 or 0.01 is 6.346 or 10.79 μm, respectively.
source: The value of λ with c = 0.1 or 0.01 is 6.346 or 10.79 μm (Figure 5B,C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C for normalized plots), respectively, showing that internalization rates of HS clusters can affect distribution ranges, as observed between Wnt and sFRPs (Mii and Taira, 2009).
evidence: This is calculated from the mathematical model and shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: Internalization rates of HS clusters can affect distribution ranges, as observed between Wnt and sFRPs.
source: The value of λ with c = 0.1 or 0.01 is 6.346 or 10.79 μm (Figure 5B,C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C for normalized plots), respectively, showing that internalization rates of HS clusters can affect distribution ranges, as observed between Wnt and sFRPs (Mii and Taira, 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the mathematical modeling and supported by a citation.

claim: When the binding rate an,max fluctuates randomly, the bound ligand component also fluctuates.
source: In our model, when the binding rate an,max (Equation 7 in the Materials and methods) fluctuates randomly (i.e. the amount of HS at position x), the bound ligand component also fluctuates (Figure 5D, blue), reproducing the local accumulation of Wnt8 and Frzb in Xenopus embryos.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The free component shows a continuously decreasing gradient even when the binding rate fluctuates randomly.
source: Even under these conditions, the free component shows a continuously decreasing gradient (Figure 5D, red), which probably corresponds to the FCS-measured, diffusing component of the FGF8 gradient in zebrafish embryos (Yu et al., 2009; measuring concentrations by FCS in a wide field is technically difficult in larger Xenopus embryos).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D and compared with literature.

claim: The mathematical model can generalize protein distributions in the extracellular space.
source: Thus, our mathematical model can generalize protein distributions in the extracellular space.
evidence: This is concluded from the modeling results.

claim: Wnt8 and Frzb colocalize with heparan sulfate clusters on cell surfaces.
source: Since Wnt8 and Frzb colocalize with heparan sulfate clusters on cell surfaces, we speculated that binding to cell surface proteins, like heparan sulfate proteoglycans (HSPGs), affects the distribution of Wnt8 and Frzb.
evidence: This is stated as a basis for the speculation about HSPG binding.

claim: 20 pg of mV-wnt8 mRNA injected into the animal cap region showed similar staining intensities to that of endogenous Wnt8 staining in the VMZ.
source: Twenty pg of mV-wnt8 mRNA injected into the animal cap region showed similar staining intensities to that of endogenous Wnt8 staining in the VMZ.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: mV-wnt8 (20 pg) showed significantly higher activities than those of TOP-FLASH only.
source: mV-wnt8 (20 pg) showed significantly higher activities than those of TOP-FLASH only, but significantly lower than those of the wild-type wnt8 (12.8 pg).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Activity of mV-Wnt8 ranges from 1/3 to 1/2 of wild-type Wnt8.
source: Activity of mV-Wnt8 ranges from 1/3 to 1/2 of wild-type Wnt8.
evidence: This is stated based on the TOP-FLASH assay results.

claim: mV-frzb showed similar activities to the wild type Frzb.
source: mV-frzb showed similar activities to the wild type Frzb.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.
